Elena — thanks for the clear asks. I routed the technical parts to Diego (infrastructure) and Marcus (security) and created two short artifacts attached. High level answers below; see attachments for diagrams and an isolation statement.

1) Noisy-neighbor mitigation (summary):
- Detection: we continuously sample per-GPU telemetry (SM utilization, memory bandwidth, SM stall, temperature, and per-process context-switch counts). Anomalies are detected by thresholds + short-window percentile spikes (95th -> 99th).
- Mitigation: automatic throttling + workload isolation. For hosted Dedicated pools we prefer hard isolation (single-tenant on physical) where requested. For multi-tenant nodes we enforce priority scheduling, per-job QoS tokens, and emergency eviction when sustained beyond thresholds (see attached run diagram).
- Eviction behavior: we perform a graceful eviction sequence: throttle -> notify customer callback -> migrate KV cache to an isolated, per-tenant cache storage (if available) -> terminate offending job only as last resort. Eviction is logged and auditable (ID, thresholds, pre/post metrics).

2) KV cache and data segregation (summary):
- KV cache is sharded per model instance and tenant. We use namespaced keys and guardrails to prevent prefix collisions. Cache memory is allocated from per-tenant pools where possible.
- Spill-to-disk / swap: we do not persist KV cache to shared disk. If a node must spill due to pressure, we write to an encrypted per-tenant ephemeral volume that is destroyed on tenant eviction.
- On eviction/swap: we zero-memory (OS-level secure-free) and run a brief scrubbing pass on any ephemeral storage before release. We log scrub completion and attach a scrub artifact where requested.

Attachments: isolation-diagram.pdf (architecture diagram), kvcache-isolation-statement.txt (security statement).

I'll let Diego add details on thresholds and tooling. If you need a short attestation letter on company letterhead we can produce one within 48 business hours.

Elena — quick technical follow-up with concrete numbers and the operational flow (keeps to SIG style). Paste of the key points below — more detail in the runbook link Mina included.

Detection metrics & thresholds (examples we use for Dedicated pools):
- GPU SM util 95th percentile > 92% for 30s window (sustained) -> mark for throttling.
- Memory bandwidth sustained > 88% for 60s -> escalate to emergency QoS.
- Per-process running threads > 2000 for 5 minutes -> signal possible runaway model.

Mitigation sequence (automated, ~30–120s depending on step):
1) Soft throttle: reduce scheduling quantum for offending process (30–60s).
2) Notify tenant via callback and create a ticket in our ops queue.
3) If sustained beyond soft window, remap offending workload to an isolated host (live migration where model supports it).
4) Final step: preempt/evict the offending container/process; collect forensic telemetry and preserve KV snapshot for owner only.

KV cache specifics:
- Namespaces: all KV keys are prefixed by tenant_id:model_id:session_id. Keyspace collisions are cryptographically prevented by including tenant-specific random nonce at model load.
- Memory & spill: KV is in GPU/host RAM. We only allow spilling to ephemeral encrypted NVMe scoped to that tenant's allocation. That volume is zeroed and detached on deallocation.
- Swap/Swapfile: we do not use OS swap in production for inference nodes; if a fallback mechanism runs it is only to encrypted per-tenant swap backed by ephemeral volumes and is scrubbed on release.

Auditing & evidence: every eviction contains a signed event (ID, node, offending PID, metrics, action taken) stored in our audit log (immutable time-series). We can provide a redacted sample audit event for your review.

If you want tighter SLAs we can offer Dedicated with strict single-tenant placement (no sharing) and a contractual eviction policy. Pricing for that mode is in our dedicated brochure.
